CCR5, or C-C chemokine receptor type 5, is best known for its role in immune cell trafficking and inflammation. Over time, researchers have recognized that the same receptor is also involved in cancer progression, particularly in metastasis and immune suppression. CCR5 is expressed on several immune cell types that tumors co-opt for their own benefit, including regulatory T cells and tumor-associated macrophages. These cells can dampen anti-tumor immune responses and create a microenvironment that supports tumor growth and spread. CCR5 functions almost like a GPS system for certain immune cells. If you disrupt that signaling, you may be able to interfere with how tumors recruit help from the immune system and how they establish metastatic niches. Why do many patients with metastatic TNBC and advanced CRC fail to respond to traditional treatments, and how does CCR5 factor into poor outcomes? TNBC and advanced CRC remain among the most difficult cancers to treat. TNBC lacks hormone receptors or HER2 (Human Epidermal Growth Factor Receptor 2) amplification, limiting targeted therapy options, while many CRC tumors, particularly microsatellite-stable disease, do not respond well to checkpoint inhibitors. In both cases, the tumor microenvironment plays a major role. These cancers often develop environments that suppress immune activity, promote resistance, and facilitate spread to distant organs. CCR5 has emerged as one factor contributing to these dynamics. By guiding immune cells that favor tumor survival and metastasis, CCR5 signaling may reinforce the very conditions that make these cancers so difficult to treat. Scientists develop monoclonal antibody therapeutics to precisely target diseased cells by engineering antibodies that recognize specific surface proteins and trigger responses, such as blocking harmful pathways or marking cells for immune destruction. ©iStock, iLexx What is leronlimab’s mechanism of action in solid tumors? Leronlimab is a humanized monoclonal antibody that binds to CCR5 and prevents it from transmitting signals. Rather than acting as a cytotoxic agent, leronlimab is intended to modulate biology upstream and downstream of the CCR5 receptor, influencing both metastatic processes and immune behavior. Leronlimab isn’t designed to poison tumor cells. It’s designed to change the rules of the environment that the tumor depends on. This has led CytoDyn to explore leronlimab primarily as a combination therapy, particularly in combination with immune checkpoint inhibitors. What have you learned so far from clinical studies of leronlimab in cancer? Across multiple programs, leronlimab demonstrates a consistent, generally well-tolerated safety profile, which enables its evaluation in oncology, infectious diseases, and metabolic conditions. In oncology, CytoDyn reported retrospective and follow-up analyses in metastatic TNBC, indicating immune-related changes, including increased Programmed Death-Ligand 1 (PD-L1) expression on circulating tumor cells and macrophage-like cells. These analyses also reported more prolonged survival in patients who received leronlimab in combination with, or following, checkpoint inhibitors, along with favorable tolerability. For example, the pooled analysis reported no dose-limiting toxicities. These findings generated hypotheses rather than confirmed them. Small sample sizes and selection effects limited interpretation. As the company has stated, the appropriate next step is prospective evaluation, which will be the focus of subsequent trials in metastatic TNBC. Continue reading below... What’s on the horizon for leronlimab, and what should people know about CytoDyn? Right now, CytoDyn is focusing on testing the biological hypotheses that emerged from earlier clinical and translational observations. Our current work with leronlimab is focused on solid tumor oncology and on understanding how CCR5 blockade may influence tumor–immune interactions in patients. An ongoing Phase 2 study in metastatic colorectal cancer is collecting both clinical outcome data and biomarker information to better understand how the tumor microenvironment changes during treatment. A Phase 2 trial in metastatic triple-negative breast cancer is also planned, designed to evaluate leronlimab in combination-based regimens while closely tracking immune markers that may help explain which patients benefit and why. Together, these studies are designed to link patient outcomes with measurable biological effects in a prospective setting. Strengthening that translational connection should help clarify leronlimab’s role and inform how it may ultimately be used alongside other cancer therapies. Up to 90 percent of compounds entering clinical trials never reach the market, often due to unforeseen toxicity or lack of efficacy in heterogenous patient populations. Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping the landscape—not only for therapeutics but also for precision diagnostics that guide patient selection and treatment decisions. Digital pathology and AI now sit at the heart of this transformation, offering new ways to extract quantitative biological signals, harmonize global lab variability, and support earlier, sharper decision‑making in clinical trials. 3 From Failure to Focus: Reducing Drug Development Risk with Computational Pathology Biology is heterogeneous, traditional pathology is variable, and global clinical trial operations introduce noise that can obscure early efficacy or safety signals. 4 Whole‑slide imaging (WSI) and computational pathology have the potential to directly address these challenges by scaling objective readouts from tissue and associated morphology with clinical outcomes. From Slides to Quantitative Biomarkers Modern AI models are capable of identifying subtle morphologic patterns that correlate with prognosis, molecular status, and treatment response. For example, multiple‑instance learning (MIL)-based approaches have matured to clinical‑grade performance for predicting histology-derived endpoints, providing objective, reproducible metrics appropriate for global deployment and regulatory evaluation. 5 These biomarkers further reduce biological uncertainty by enabling earlier biological signal detection and quantitative features that can be deployed consistently across global trials. This shift allows development teams to detect trends long before traditional clinical endpoints mature. 6 Strengthening Oncology Trial Decisions Through Early AI‑Enabled Signal Detection AI‑enabled biomarkers support early patient stratification, reduce biological and operational noise, and enable more accurate response prediction across oncology trials . Increasingly, studies demonstrate that morphology‑derived signatures extracted from routine histology can predict outcomes and drug response earlier—and often more reproducibly—than traditional clinical readouts. 6 This is particularly relevant in immuno‑oncology, where response to therapy is shaped by both tumor-intrinsic features and the tumor microenvironment. While established biomarkers such as PD‑L1 immunohistochemistry have been central to patient selection, they only capture part of this biological complexity. In this context, weakly supervised AI models applied to standard H&E sections can infer tumor microenvironment characteristics and immunotherapy response at scale, complementing PD-L1 based strategies and enabling earlier enrichment and informed decisions for treatment optimization. 3,6 Bridging the R&D–to–Real‑World Gap in CDx Development Companion diagnostics (CDx) failures often occur not during discovery, but at deployment—when real‑world laboratory variability undermines analytical performance. Multi‑center datasets consistently demonstrate significant inter-laboratory variation in staining and scanning, driving domain shift and degrading model performance unless proactively managed. 7 Recent studies underscore how stain‑normalization techniques are evolving to address this challenge. Methods such as Macenko, Reinhard, and Vahadane continue to serve as strong and reliable baselines, sustaining their role as workhorses in digital pathology workflows. In parallel, generative adversarial network‑based and hybrid approaches are demonstrating clear advantages in cross‑site robustness, enabling models to generalize more effectively across heterogeneous scanners and staining protocols. Most notably, techniques, such as stain‑aware normalization and Beer–Lambert-based models, offer substantial reductions in performance loss under shifting staining conditions, representing a meaningful advance toward more resilient and deployment‑ready image analysis pipelines. These capabilities are critical for achieving analytically valid CDx deployment across global laboratory networks. 8 Infrastructure Readiness: Cloud‑Native, Compliant, and Audit‑Ready Digital pathology infrastructure continues to mature globally, with cloud‑native, compliant, and fully auditable platforms emerging as the foundation for scalable deployment. The FDA clearance of WSI for primary diagnosis has further facilitated adoption, enabling clinical‑grade digital pathology infrastructure to operate reliably and securely across institutions. Importantly, the infrastructure readiness in AI-enabled pathology extends beyond software and cloud architecture to the full end-to-end system, from tissue handling to computational analysis. At present, glass slides remain the biological ground truth, supporting regulatory review, retrospective analysis, and future biomarker discovery. Not all whole-slide scanners are equivalent in optical quality, color fidelity, throughput, or reproducibility. These differences can have a significant impact on downstream algorithm performance if not carefully controlled. As AI-derived endpoints move into registrational trials and companion diagnostic deployment, the selection of clinically validated, high-performance scanning platforms become a critical component of infrastructure readiness. In parallel, regulatory expectations for AI in healthcare are becoming increasingly well defined, with greater emphasis on adherence to Good Machine Learning Practice (GMLP), transparency in AI‑generated outputs, and robust oversight across the total product lifecycle—including proactive post‑market monitoring.  For AI-enabled assays, this includes controls such as cell line and reference material controls, locked models, cross-lab performance monitoring, and auditable data lineage. Cloud‑native pipelines, designed to meet HIPAA/GDPR requirements, can now offer essential capabilities such as comprehensive audit trails, encryption, role‑based access control, and data lineage. Jacob Lalezari , PhD Chief Executive Officer CytoDyn In this Innovation Spotlight, Jacob Lalezari from CytoDyn discusses how next-generation monoclonal antibodies have the potential to improve clinical outcomes of difficult-to-treat diseases. He explains the mechanism of action of leronlimab, a humanized monoclonal antibody that functions as a CCR5 antagonist and highlights its promise for treating solid tumors , specifically metastatic triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) and advanced colorectal cancer (CRC). What is next-generation monoclonal antibody therapy, and what benefits has it provided to cancer patients? Monoclonal antibodies have been a mainstay of cancer therapy for decades, but the field has evolved well beyond the early days of single-target binding. Next-generation antibody therapies are designed to be more versatile, capable of delivering drugs directly to tumors, engaging multiple immune pathways, as with leronlimab, or persisting longer in circulation to sustain therapeutic effects. In oncology, we’re moving away from the idea that one mechanism alone is enough. The next wave of antibodies is about influencing biology in a more integrated way, how tumors interact with the immune system, how they spread, and how they resist treatment. Clinically, this shift has led to more precise therapies and, in some cases, improved outcomes, particularly when antibodies are combined with other agents. CytoDyn’s work with leronlimab aligns with this broader trend, focusing not on direct tumor killing but on altering the biological conditions that allow cancer to progress. Continue reading below... CCR5, or C-C chemokine receptor type 5, is best known for its role in immune cell trafficking and inflammation. Over time, researchers have recognized that the same receptor is also involved in cancer progression, particularly in metastasis and immune suppression. CCR5 is expressed on several immune cell types that tumors co-opt for their own benefit, including regulatory T cells and tumor-associated macrophages. These cells can dampen anti-tumor immune responses and create a microenvironment that supports tumor growth and spread. CCR5 functions almost like a GPS system for certain immune cells. If you disrupt that signaling, you may be able to interfere with how tumors recruit help from the immune system and how they establish metastatic niches. Why do many patients with metastatic TNBC and advanced CRC fail to respond to traditional treatments, and how does CCR5 factor into poor outcomes? TNBC and advanced CRC remain among the most difficult cancers to treat. TNBC lacks hormone receptors or HER2 (Human Epidermal Growth Factor Receptor 2) amplification, limiting targeted therapy options, while many CRC tumors, particularly microsatellite-stable disease, do not respond well to checkpoint inhibitors. In both cases, the tumor microenvironment plays a major role. These cancers often develop environments that suppress immune activity, promote resistance, and facilitate spread to distant organs. CCR5 has emerged as one factor contributing to these dynamics. By guiding immune cells that favor tumor survival and metastasis, CCR5 signaling may reinforce the very conditions that make these cancers so difficult to treat. Scientists develop monoclonal antibody therapeutics to precisely target diseased cells by engineering antibodies that recognize specific surface proteins and trigger responses, such as blocking harmful pathways or marking cells for immune destruction. ©iStock, iLexx What is leronlimab’s mechanism of action in solid tumors? Leronlimab is a humanized monoclonal antibody that binds to CCR5 and prevents it from transmitting signals. Rather than acting as a cytotoxic agent, leronlimab is intended to modulate biology upstream and downstream of the CCR5 receptor, influencing both metastatic processes and immune behavior. Leronlimab isn’t designed to poison tumor cells. It’s designed to change the rules of the environment that the tumor depends on. This has led CytoDyn to explore leronlimab primarily as a combination therapy, particularly in combination with immune checkpoint inhibitors. What have you learned so far from clinical studies of leronlimab in cancer? Across multiple programs, leronlimab demonstrates a consistent, generally well-tolerated safety profile, which enables its evaluation in oncology, infectious diseases, and metabolic conditions. In oncology, CytoDyn reported retrospective and follow-up analyses in metastatic TNBC, indicating immune-related changes, including increased Programmed Death-Ligand 1 (PD-L1) expression on circulating tumor cells and macrophage-like cells. These analyses also reported more prolonged survival in patients who received leronlimab in combination with, or following, checkpoint inhibitors, along with favorable tolerability. For example, the pooled analysis reported no dose-limiting toxicities. These findings generated hypotheses rather than confirmed them. Small sample sizes and selection effects limited interpretation. As the company has stated, the appropriate next step is prospective evaluation, which will be the focus of subsequent trials in metastatic TNBC. Continue reading below... The goal is to move from biologically intriguing observations to clinically testable hypotheses in a CRC subgroup that historically responded poorly to immunotherapy alone. What’s on the horizon for leronlimab, and what should people know about CytoDyn? Right now, CytoDyn is focusing on testing the biological hypotheses that emerged from earlier clinical and translational observations. Our current work with leronlimab is focused on solid tumor oncology and on understanding how CCR5 blockade may influence tumor–immune interactions in patients. An ongoing Phase 2 study in metastatic colorectal cancer is collecting both clinical outcome data and biomarker information to better understand how the tumor microenvironment changes during treatment. A Phase 2 trial in metastatic triple-negative breast cancer is also planned, designed to evaluate leronlimab in combination-based regimens while closely tracking immune markers that may help explain which patients benefit and why. Together, these studies are designed to link patient outcomes with measurable biological effects in a prospective setting. Strengthening that translational connection should help clarify leronlimab’s role and inform how it may ultimately be used alongside other cancer therapies. Image credit: © iStock.com, Yuuji PDF version Register for free to listen to this article Listen with Speechify 0:00 7:00 Share T he path to bringing a new drug to market is increasingly complex and costly, with development costs now exceeding $2 billion and timelines approaching a decade. 1,2 The stakes have never been higher—demanding new models, new technologies, and new thinking to reduce risk and accelerate breakthroughs. Up to 90 percent of compounds entering clinical trials never reach the market, often due to unforeseen toxicity or lack of efficacy in heterogenous patient populations. This high failure rate has accelerated a shift toward more targeted development strategies. Companion diagnostics are central to this shift, enabling more precise trials, faster development cycles, and better health outcomes for some of the world’s sickest patients. Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping the landscape—not only for therapeutics but also for precision diagnostics that guide patient selection and treatment decisions. Digital pathology and AI now sit at the heart of this transformation, offering new ways to extract quantitative biological signals, harmonize global lab variability, and support earlier, sharper decision‑making in clinical trials. 3 From Failure to Focus: Reducing Drug Development Risk with Computational Pathology Biology is heterogeneous, traditional pathology is variable, and global clinical trial operations introduce noise that can obscure early efficacy or safety signals. 4 Whole‑slide imaging (WSI) and computational pathology have the potential to directly address these challenges by scaling objective readouts from tissue and associated morphology with clinical outcomes. Continue reading below... Like this story? Sign up for FREE Cancer updates: Latest science news stories Topic-tailored resources and events Customized newsletter content Subscribe With over 15 years of experience in diagnostics and pathology, I have seen how “identical” hematoxylin & eosin (H&E) slides can vary across sites—introducing noise, repeat reviews, and delayed decisions. This becomes particularly challenging when variability forces the tissue journey to restart, or worse, necessitates repeat tissue collection from patients, many of whom are critically ill—consuming precious, often irreplaceable patient samples and driving additional trial costs. AI‑enabled tissue quantification has the potential to address these challenges by reducing subjectivity, delivering more reproducible endpoints, and generating cleaner data earlier in drug development. AI can also serve as a second set of eyes during review, helping ensure critical features are not missed and increasing confidence in study outcomes. From Slides to Quantitative Biomarkers Modern AI models are capable of identifying subtle morphologic patterns that correlate with prognosis, molecular status, and treatment response. For example, multiple‑instance learning (MIL)-based approaches have matured to clinical‑grade performance for predicting histology-derived endpoints, providing objective, reproducible metrics appropriate for global deployment and regulatory evaluation. 5 These biomarkers further reduce biological uncertainty by enabling earlier biological signal detection and quantitative features that can be deployed consistently across global trials. This shift allows development teams to detect trends long before traditional clinical endpoints mature. 6 Strengthening Oncology Trial Decisions Through Early AI‑Enabled Signal Detection AI‑enabled biomarkers support early patient stratification, reduce biological and operational noise, and enable more accurate response prediction across oncology trials . Increasingly, studies demonstrate that morphology‑derived signatures extracted from routine histology can predict outcomes and drug response earlier—and often more reproducibly—than traditional clinical readouts. 6 This is particularly relevant in immuno‑oncology, where response to therapy is shaped by both tumor-intrinsic features and the tumor microenvironment. While established biomarkers such as PD‑L1 immunohistochemistry have been central to patient selection, they only capture part of this biological complexity. In this context, weakly supervised AI models applied to standard H&E sections can infer tumor microenvironment characteristics and immunotherapy response at scale, complementing PD-L1 based strategies and enabling earlier enrichment and informed decisions for treatment optimization. 3,6 Bridging the R&D–to–Real‑World Gap in CDx Development Companion diagnostics (CDx) failures often occur not during discovery, but at deployment—when real‑world laboratory variability undermines analytical performance. Multi‑center datasets consistently demonstrate significant inter-laboratory variation in staining and scanning, driving domain shift and degrading model performance unless proactively managed. 7 Recent studies underscore how stain‑normalization techniques are evolving to address this challenge. Methods such as Macenko, Reinhard, and Vahadane continue to serve as strong and reliable baselines, sustaining their role as workhorses in digital pathology workflows. In parallel, generative adversarial network‑based and hybrid approaches are demonstrating clear advantages in cross‑site robustness, enabling models to generalize more effectively across heterogeneous scanners and staining protocols. Most notably, techniques, such as stain‑aware normalization and Beer–Lambert-based models, offer substantial reductions in performance loss under shifting staining conditions, representing a meaningful advance toward more resilient and deployment‑ready image analysis pipelines. These capabilities are critical for achieving analytically valid CDx deployment across global laboratory networks. 8 Infrastructure Readiness: Cloud‑Native, Compliant, and Audit‑Ready Digital pathology infrastructure continues to mature globally, with cloud‑native, compliant, and fully auditable platforms emerging as the foundation for scalable deployment. The FDA clearance of WSI for primary diagnosis has further facilitated adoption, enabling clinical‑grade digital pathology infrastructure to operate reliably and securely across institutions. Importantly, the infrastructure readiness in AI-enabled pathology extends beyond software and cloud architecture to the full end-to-end system, from tissue handling to computational analysis. At present, glass slides remain the biological ground truth, supporting regulatory review, retrospective analysis, and future biomarker discovery. Not all whole-slide scanners are equivalent in optical quality, color fidelity, throughput, or reproducibility. These differences can have a significant impact on downstream algorithm performance if not carefully controlled. As AI-derived endpoints move into registrational trials and companion diagnostic deployment, the selection of clinically validated, high-performance scanning platforms become a critical component of infrastructure readiness. In parallel, regulatory expectations for AI in healthcare are becoming increasingly well defined, with greater emphasis on adherence to Good Machine Learning Practice (GMLP), transparency in AI‑generated outputs, and robust oversight across the total product lifecycle—including proactive post‑market monitoring.  For AI-enabled assays, this includes controls such as cell line and reference material controls, locked models, cross-lab performance monitoring, and auditable data lineage. Cloud‑native pipelines, designed to meet HIPAA/GDPR requirements, can now offer essential capabilities such as comprehensive audit trails, encryption, role‑based access control, and data lineage. Together, these developments support deployment-ready, regulator-aligned digital pathology workflows for next-generation companion diagnostics and clinical decision support. Regional CDx Regulatory Landscape In the US, the FDA provides relatively clear CDx co‑development pathways , supported by oncology‑focused pilot programs that encourage early alignment between therapeutic and diagnostic development. In Europe, the In Vitro Diagnostic Regulation (IVDR) elevates CDx to Class C, requiring Notified Body review and consultation with the European Medicines Agency . While this shift strengthens regulatory rigor and oversight, it also introduces increased workload, operational complexity, and longer development timelines. Comparative analyses show widening differences between FDA and IVDR requirements—underscoring the importance of coordinated, early regulatory planning. Without proactive alignment, these regional differences can introduce delays, rework, and downstream risk to global CDx deployment. AI Augmenting Pathologists Workflows AI has the potential to improve diagnostic accuracy, standardization, and efficiency in pathology. However, contextual interpretation, clinical judgement, and patient‑impacting decisions remain firmly within the expertise of the pathologist. Reviews continue to emphasize that safe and effective use of AI requires clinician‑in‑the‑loop workflows, where human oversight is integral to decision‑making. 9,10 As a cyto- and histopathologist, I have spent countless hours performing manual, time‑intensive tasks such as accurately counting inflammatory cells to diagnose acute bladder inflammation or enumerating mitotic figures to determine breast cancer grade, decisions that directly influence patient treatment. AI has the potential to relieve pathologists of these repetitive, low-value tasks, allowing us to focus on integrative reasoning, clinical context, and complex diagnostic synthesis—capabilities that algorithms cannot replicate. The Future: Multimodal, Generalizable, and Equitable Next‑generation multimodal foundation models integrate histology with clinical reports, genomics, and proteomics to improve disease classification, survival prediction, and biological interpretability across cancer types. These models move beyond single‑modality analysis, enabling richer context and more biologically meaningful insights. 8 When rigorously validated across sites and paired with stain‑robust deployment‑ready pipelines, these systems have the potential to expand access to precision diagnostics globally, including in low‑resource settings where specialist expertise and advanced infrastructure may be limited. 3,11 Importantly, AI is not a substitute for skilled laboratory staff and researchers; rather it serves as a powerful second set of eyes—enhancing precision, increasing agility, and elevating the quality of scientific work with deeper insights. Collaboration Delivers Greater Value In an environment where accelerating time‑to‑market is increasingly critical, building diagnostics capabilities from scratch can introduce unnecessary cost, delay, and execution risk. Strategic collaboration offers a more efficient path forward, allowing innovation to scale without sacrificing rigor or speed. Beyond operational efficiency, collaboration also enables a departure from traditional CDx partnership models that often constrain speed and flexibility. Emerging platform-based, data-centric approaches allow therapeutic and diagnostic development to progress in parallel, reducing hand-offs, compressing timelines, and enabling faster launches. Importantly, these models support earlier alignment on evidence generation, regulatory strategy, and global deployment—reducing late-stage friction that has historically delayed market entry. Partnerships are helping build comprehensive antibody libraries, powered by sophisticated AI analysis. Instead of starting anew, pharmaceutical companies can leverage robust, pre‑validated datasets to establish proof‑of‑concept more rapidly and with greater confidence. For emerging biomarkers, the platform’s ability to generate custom antibodies on demand adds critical flexibility and speed. Looking Ahead: A New Model for Evidence Generation As personalized medicine becomes the standard of care, the pressure on pharmaceutical companies to develop robust companion diagnostics has never been greater—elevating risk mitigation capabilities from operational considerations to sources of competitive advantage. AI is emerging as the new scientific lens for drug development and CDx. By reducing biological uncertainty, harmonizing variability across global laboratory networks, and supporting earlier, more confident decision‑making, AI is accelerating the path from discovery to meaningful patient impact. Critically, the next evolution of evidence generation will integrate real-world evidence (RWE) with clinical trial data. When combined with AI-enabled diagnostics, RWE enables ongoing validation of biomarker performance across more diverse patient populations, strengthening confidence in clinical utility beyond controlled trials. This approach allows best practices to be scaled more rapidly, accelerating the translation of approved innovations into meaningful patient impact. As cloud‑based pathology infrastructure continues to mature and regulatory frameworks for AI diagnostics evolve, these technologies will increasingly define how evidence is generated, validated, and translated into the next generation of precision therapeutics. Feb 14, 2026 | 4 min read Save for Later Researchers develop next-generation monoclonal antibody treatments with specialized binding arms that target disease more effectively than traditional antibodies. Image credit: ©iStock, nopparit PDF version Share Researchers engineer monoclonal antibodies to selectively bind disease-associated proteins, enabling targeted prevention, detection, and treatment across multiple therapeutic areas. Unlike small-molecule drugs, which often interact with multiple biological pathways, these antibodies achieve higher target specificity through their unique antigen-recognition domains with lower off-target effects. Advances in antibody engineering, such as humanization and affinity maturation, expand therapeutic applications to previously intractable diseases. Jacob Lalezari , PhD Chief Executive Officer CytoDyn In this Innovation Spotlight, Jacob Lalezari from CytoDyn discusses how next-generation monoclonal antibodies have the potential to improve clinical outcomes of difficult-to-treat diseases. He explains the mechanism of action of leronlimab, a humanized monoclonal antibody that functions as a CCR5 antagonist and highlights its promise for treating solid tumors , specifically metastatic triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) and advanced colorectal cancer (CRC). What is next-generation monoclonal antibody therapy, and what benefits has it provided to cancer patients? Monoclonal antibodies have been a mainstay of cancer therapy for decades, but the field has evolved well beyond the early days of single-target binding. Next-generation antibody therapies are designed to be more versatile, capable of delivering drugs directly to tumors, engaging multiple immune pathways, as with leronlimab, or persisting longer in circulation to sustain therapeutic effects. In oncology, we’re moving away from the idea that one mechanism alone is enough. The next wave of antibodies is about influencing biology in a more integrated way, how tumors interact with the immune system, how they spread, and how they resist treatment. Clinically, this shift has led to more precise therapies and, in some cases, improved outcomes, particularly when antibodies are combined with other agents. CytoDyn’s work with leronlimab aligns with this broader trend, focusing not on direct tumor killing but on altering the biological conditions that allow cancer to progress. Continue reading below... Like this story? Sign up for FREE Immunology updates: Latest science news stories Topic-tailored resources and events Customized newsletter content Subscribe What is CCR5, and why is it considered a promising cancer target? CCR5, or C-C chemokine receptor type 5, is best known for its role in immune cell trafficking and inflammation. Over time, researchers have recognized that the same receptor is also involved in cancer progression, particularly in metastasis and immune suppression. CCR5 is expressed on several immune cell types that tumors co-opt for their own benefit, including regulatory T cells and tumor-associated macrophages. These cells can dampen anti-tumor immune responses and create a microenvironment that supports tumor growth and spread. CCR5 functions almost like a GPS system for certain immune cells. If you disrupt that signaling, you may be able to interfere with how tumors recruit help from the immune system and how they establish metastatic niches. Why do many patients with metastatic TNBC and advanced CRC fail to respond to traditional treatments, and how does CCR5 factor into poor outcomes? TNBC and advanced CRC remain among the most difficult cancers to treat. TNBC lacks hormone receptors or HER2 (Human Epidermal Growth Factor Receptor 2) amplification, limiting targeted therapy options, while many CRC tumors, particularly microsatellite-stable disease, do not respond well to checkpoint inhibitors. In both cases, the tumor microenvironment plays a major role. These cancers often develop environments that suppress immune activity, promote resistance, and facilitate spread to distant organs. CCR5 has emerged as one factor contributing to these dynamics. By guiding immune cells that favor tumor survival and metastasis, CCR5 signaling may reinforce the very conditions that make these cancers so difficult to treat. Scientists develop monoclonal antibody therapeutics to precisely target diseased cells by engineering antibodies that recognize specific surface proteins and trigger responses, such as blocking harmful pathways or marking cells for immune destruction. ©iStock, iLexx What is leronlimab’s mechanism of action in solid tumors? Leronlimab is a humanized monoclonal antibody that binds to CCR5 and prevents it from transmitting signals. Rather than acting as a cytotoxic agent, leronlimab is intended to modulate biology upstream and downstream of the CCR5 receptor, influencing both metastatic processes and immune behavior. Leronlimab isn’t designed to poison tumor cells. It’s designed to change the rules of the environment that the tumor depends on. This has led CytoDyn to explore leronlimab primarily as a combination therapy, particularly in combination with immune checkpoint inhibitors. What have you learned so far from clinical studies of leronlimab in cancer? Across multiple programs, leronlimab demonstrates a consistent, generally well-tolerated safety profile, which enables its evaluation in oncology, infectious diseases, and metabolic conditions. In oncology, CytoDyn reported retrospective and follow-up analyses in metastatic TNBC, indicating immune-related changes, including increased Programmed Death-Ligand 1 (PD-L1) expression on circulating tumor cells and macrophage-like cells. These analyses also reported more prolonged survival in patients who received leronlimab in combination with, or following, checkpoint inhibitors, along with favorable tolerability. For example, the pooled analysis reported no dose-limiting toxicities. These findings generated hypotheses rather than confirmed them. Small sample sizes and selection effects limited interpretation. As the company has stated, the appropriate next step is prospective evaluation, which will be the focus of subsequent trials in metastatic TNBC. Continue reading below... Read More CytoDyn publicly reported FDA discussions supporting a Phase 2 approach in CCR5-positive, microsatellite-stable, metastatic CRC , combining leronlimab with standard agents. The goal is to move from biologically intriguing observations to clinically testable hypotheses in a CRC subgroup that historically responded poorly to immunotherapy alone. What’s on the horizon for leronlimab, and what should people know about CytoDyn? Right now, CytoDyn is focusing on testing the biological hypotheses that emerged from earlier clinical and translational observations. Our current work with leronlimab is focused on solid tumor oncology and on understanding how CCR5 blockade may influence tumor–immune interactions in patients. An ongoing Phase 2 study in metastatic colorectal cancer is collecting both clinical outcome data and biomarker information to better understand how the tumor microenvironment changes during treatment. A Phase 2 trial in metastatic triple-negative breast cancer is also planned, designed to evaluate leronlimab in combination-based regimens while closely tracking immune markers that may help explain which patients benefit and why. Together, these studies are designed to link patient outcomes with measurable biological effects in a prospective setting. Strengthening that translational connection should help clarify leronlimab’s role and inform how it may ultimately be used alongside other cancer therapies. Researchers develop next-generation monoclonal antibody treatments with specialized binding arms that target disease more effectively than traditional antibodies. Image credit: ©iStock, nopparit PDF version Share Researchers engineer monoclonal antibodies to selectively bind disease-associated proteins, enabling targeted prevention, detection, and treatment across multiple therapeutic areas. Unlike small-molecule drugs, which often interact with multiple biological pathways, these antibodies achieve higher target specificity through their unique antigen-recognition domains with lower off-target effects. Advances in antibody engineering, such as humanization and affinity maturation, expand therapeutic applications to previously intractable diseases. Jacob Lalezari , PhD Chief Executive Officer CytoDyn In this Innovation Spotlight, Jacob Lalezari from CytoDyn discusses how next-generation monoclonal antibodies have the potential to improve clinical outcomes of difficult-to-treat diseases. He explains the mechanism of action of leronlimab, a humanized monoclonal antibody that functions as a CCR5 antagonist and highlights its promise for treating solid tumors , specifically metastatic triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) and advanced colorectal cancer (CRC). What is next-generation monoclonal antibody therapy, and what benefits has it provided to cancer patients? Monoclonal antibodies have been a mainstay of cancer therapy for decades, but the field has evolved well beyond the early days of single-target binding. Next-generation antibody therapies are designed to be more versatile, capable of delivering drugs directly to tumors, engaging multiple immune pathways, as with leronlimab, or persisting longer in circulation to sustain therapeutic effects. In oncology, we’re moving away from the idea that one mechanism alone is enough. The next wave of antibodies is about influencing biology in a more integrated way, how tumors interact with the immune system, how they spread, and how they resist treatment. Clinically, this shift has led to more precise therapies and, in some cases, improved outcomes, particularly when antibodies are combined with other agents. CytoDyn’s work with leronlimab aligns with this broader trend, focusing not on direct tumor killing but on altering the biological conditions that allow cancer to progress. Continue reading below... CCR5, or C-C chemokine receptor type 5, is best known for its role in immune cell trafficking and inflammation. Over time, researchers have recognized that the same receptor is also involved in cancer progression, particularly in metastasis and immune suppression. CCR5 is expressed on several immune cell types that tumors co-opt for their own benefit, including regulatory T cells and tumor-associated macrophages. These cells can dampen anti-tumor immune responses and create a microenvironment that supports tumor growth and spread. CCR5 functions almost like a GPS system for certain immune cells. If you disrupt that signaling, you may be able to interfere with how tumors recruit help from the immune system and how they establish metastatic niches. Why do many patients with metastatic TNBC and advanced CRC fail to respond to traditional treatments, and how does CCR5 factor into poor outcomes? TNBC and advanced CRC remain among the most difficult cancers to treat. TNBC lacks hormone receptors or HER2 (Human Epidermal Growth Factor Receptor 2) amplification, limiting targeted therapy options, while many CRC tumors, particularly microsatellite-stable disease, do not respond well to checkpoint inhibitors. In both cases, the tumor microenvironment plays a major role. These cancers often develop environments that suppress immune activity, promote resistance, and facilitate spread to distant organs. CCR5 has emerged as one factor contributing to these dynamics. By guiding immune cells that favor tumor survival and metastasis, CCR5 signaling may reinforce the very conditions that make these cancers so difficult to treat. Scientists develop monoclonal antibody therapeutics to precisely target diseased cells by engineering antibodies that recognize specific surface proteins and trigger responses, such as blocking harmful pathways or marking cells for immune destruction. ©iStock, iLexx What is leronlimab’s mechanism of action in solid tumors? Leronlimab is a humanized monoclonal antibody that binds to CCR5 and prevents it from transmitting signals. Rather than acting as a cytotoxic agent, leronlimab is intended to modulate biology upstream and downstream of the CCR5 receptor, influencing both metastatic processes and immune behavior. Leronlimab isn’t designed to poison tumor cells. It’s designed to change the rules of the environment that the tumor depends on. This has led CytoDyn to explore leronlimab primarily as a combination therapy, particularly in combination with immune checkpoint inhibitors. What have you learned so far from clinical studies of leronlimab in cancer? Across multiple programs, leronlimab demonstrates a consistent, generally well-tolerated safety profile, which enables its evaluation in oncology, infectious diseases, and metabolic conditions. In oncology, CytoDyn reported retrospective and follow-up analyses in metastatic TNBC, indicating immune-related changes, including increased Programmed Death-Ligand 1 (PD-L1) expression on circulating tumor cells and macrophage-like cells. These analyses also reported more prolonged survival in patients who received leronlimab in combination with, or following, checkpoint inhibitors, along with favorable tolerability. For example, the pooled analysis reported no dose-limiting toxicities. These findings generated hypotheses rather than confirmed them. Small sample sizes and selection effects limited interpretation. As the company has stated, the appropriate next step is prospective evaluation, which will be the focus of subsequent trials in metastatic TNBC. Continue reading below... Read More CytoDyn publicly reported FDA discussions supporting a Phase 2 approach in CCR5-positive, microsatellite-stable, metastatic CRC , combining leronlimab with standard agents. The goal is to move from biologically intriguing observations to clinically testable hypotheses in a CRC subgroup that historically responded poorly to immunotherapy alone. What’s on the horizon for leronlimab, and what should people know about CytoDyn? Right now, CytoDyn is focusing on testing the biological hypotheses that emerged from earlier clinical and translational observations. Our current work with leronlimab is focused on solid tumor oncology and on understanding how CCR5 blockade may influence tumor–immune interactions in patients. An ongoing Phase 2 study in metastatic colorectal cancer is collecting both clinical outcome data and biomarker information to better understand how the tumor microenvironment changes during treatment. A Phase 2 trial in metastatic triple-negative breast cancer is also planned, designed to evaluate leronlimab in combination-based regimens while closely tracking immune markers that may help explain which patients benefit and why. Together, these studies are designed to link patient outcomes with measurable biological effects in a prospective setting. Strengthening that translational connection should help clarify leronlimab’s role and inform how it may ultimately be used alongside other cancer therapies.
